edits.value_json: 面 is interpreted as a face picture, with an eye inside an outline. It commonly means “face” and also has recorded senses such as “surface” and “side.” In simplified Chinese, it also writes the flour and noodle word written 麵 in traditional Chinese.

Pictographic: the oracle graph has competing analyses. One reads it as an eye inside a face outline; another reads it as 目 within an outline, while the received Shuowen account relates 面 to 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. The ancient construction and graphic transitions remain disputed.

面 is treated here as one pictorial graph. One analysis reads an eye within a face outline; another assigns the inner form to 目 and the outer form to a face outline. The received Shuowen account instead relates the graph to 𦣻; these analyses do not establish separate current components.

The cited scholarly account distinguishes oracle forms interpreted as 目 inside an outer face outline from Western Zhou bronze forms used only as a component and interpreted there as a head-related form with an indicator for the face. It describes the Chu-slip form as apparently developing from the Western Zhou shape, and later Qin, seal and early Han forms as combining developments from oracle and Western Zhou shapes. These interpretations do not establish a single graphic sequence.

The received Shuowen explanation relates 面 to 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. The cited paleographic accounts disagree about how this later head-related analysis relates to the oracle forms; 靣 is recorded as a variant, with no established ancestry linking it to 面.

The individual oracle inscriptions and their dates were not verified. Scholarly analyses disagree over the inner element and its relation to the later 𦣻/首 analysis; proposed graphic pathways remain unresolved. The report that 面 is absent from bronze inscriptions does not specify the surveyed corpus’s limits.
Dates and links among the facing, surface, side, and dimension uses remain unresolved; the cited facing use does not by itself establish a semantic development from “face.”

The relationship between 面 and 麵 as spellings is supported, but the exact chronology of 麪 and 麵 and the separate earliest attestations of flour and noodle senses remain unresolved. The evidence does not establish borrowing of the food word from the face word.
